regions.name: Colorado Front Range
regions.blurb: Cameron Peak and East Troublesome: the two largest fires in Colorado history, plus CalWood above Boulder. Forest fuels; East Troublesome grew by about 87,000 acres in a single day.

regions.name: Northern California
regions.blurb: The August 2020 lightning siege. The August Complex began as dozens of separate lightning ignitions that grew together, so even the official record has to decide what counts as one fire.

regions.name: Oregon Cascades
regions.blurb: The Labor Day 2020 east-wind event: Beachie Creek, Lionshead, Riverside, Holiday Farm and Archie Creek. Fires that burned for weeks then exploded in a single night.

regions.name: Central & Southern Arizona
regions.blurb: Desert grassland, chaparral and sky-island forest: the Bush and Bighorn fires alongside many smaller fires, with very different fuels sitting close together.

regions.name: Southwest Idaho
regions.blurb: Sagebrush steppe on the Snake River Plain around Boise. Rangeland fires driven by cheatgrass can cover huge areas in a day or two, then go out.

regions.name: Kansas Flint Hills
regions.blurb: Tallgrass prairie with intensive spring prescribed burning: thousands of small, adjacent, deliberately lit fires. No perimeters exist for most of them.

regions.name: Central Kalimantan, Indonesia
regions.blurb: Tropical peatland and the former Mega Rice Project, where Cattau's clustering algorithm was first applied. 2019 was a severe El Niño fire year; no national perimeter or ignition records exist.
